key_insight: The paper argues that apparent triage errors come from how the model converts an already-preserved clinical representation into a multiple-choice answer, not from loss of medical understanding.
clinical_relevance: For clinical NLP benchmarking, output format can substantially change measured triage performance, so free-text vs. multiple-choice results should not be interpreted as equivalent.
method: Compared sparse-autoencoder features across free-text and multiple-choice settings in Gemma 3 4B/12B IT and Qwen3-8B.
Used natural-language autoencoder verbalization, decision-token logit attribution, and top-feature characterization to identify what drives answers.
Tested behavioral effects with structured and natural-language inputs plus option-order shuffling.
evidence_signal: Across the shared clinical narrative, medical features were active in both formats but went silent at the multiple-choice decision token, while scaffold/format features dominated decision logits and the gap was largely due to adjacent-letter off-by-one choices.
watch_item: These findings suggest benchmark scores may reflect format sensitivity rather than clinical capability, so any deployment or evaluation should avoid overgeneralizing from constrained multiple-choice triage tasks.
paper_title: Internal Representation, Not Clinical Knowledge: Where Apparent LLM Triage Failures Originate
